passage: Uday Mama poured the tea and looked at Kunal. "You think you're the first to have doubts? When I was sixteen, I stopped going to the temple with my father. Not because I hated it. I just didn't know if I believed what I was saying. So I read. I went to the gurdwara with my friend Harjit, to the church near our school at Christmas, sat at the dargah on Thursdays. I argued with everyone, including my father. It took me three years. In the end I went back to the temple, but not the same way. I pray now because I've chosen it, not because I was told. And I still read other books." Kunal turned his cup. "Did your father get angry?" "At first. Later he asked me what I'd read."

qa.q: Where did young Uday go with his friend Harjit?
qa.a: To the gurdwara.

qa.q: How did young Uday feel when he stopped going to the temple with his father?
qa.a: He felt unsure and uneasy, not knowing whether he believed what he was saying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Uday's search, and what did he gain from it?
qa.a: Choosing to read and visit different places of worship; he came back to prayer as his own choice instead of just habit.

qa.q: How might Uday's father have felt during those three years?
qa.a: At first he was angry, perhaps worried his son was drifting, but later he became curious about what Uday had read.

grounding: An uncle recalls exploring several faiths as a teenager before choosing his own relationship with belief.

passage: The mock parliament hall was noisy, the fans weren't working, and Saurabh had four minutes before he had to speak on the plastic ban bill. His father thought the ban was bad for small shopkeepers, and at home Saurabh had always agreed. But for two weeks he'd been reading, and talking to the vegetable seller who said the ban had actually cut her costs. Zeenat, his partner, leaned over. "Which side are you really on?" He looked at his notes, crossed out a line, and wrote a new one. When his name was called, he stood up. "I support the ban, with help for small sellers." His voice shook a little. Zeenat grinned. Later, on the bus, he texted his father: "Can we talk about it tonight? I changed my mind, sort of."

qa.q: How many minutes did Saurabh have before he spoke?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when his voice shook?
qa.a: He was nervous, speaking a view of his own for the first time, one that differed from his father's.

qa.q: Which parts of how Saurabh reached his position were wise?
qa.a: He read for two weeks and listened to someone affected, instead of just repeating what he'd heard at home.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's father feel about the text?
qa.a: He might feel surprised, possibly defensive, but also curious to hear how his son's thinking changed.

grounding: A teenager commits to his own researched position in a mock parliament, differing from his father's view.

I returned Sabina's lab report with comments: good data, but the conclusion claimed more than the results show. At first she argued. "But everyone writes it like that, Sir." passage: The night before board results, the power went off in the Ranchi flat. The heat pressed down. Ojas, seventeen, sat on the balcony in the dark, his phone at five percent. "What's even the point of all this studying," he muttered. "Marks, college, then what? Everyone's stressed. The world's on fire." His sister Bhavna came out with two glasses of water. She sat beside him. "Say more." He did: the results, the news, the feeling that nothing he did would change anything out there. She listened. "That's a lot to carry at midnight." "It is." "Tomorrow, after results, whatever they are, will you talk to the school counsellor with me? I went last year." Ojas nodded slowly. "Okay." They sat together until the fan came back on.

qa.q: What percentage was Ojas's phone at?
qa.a: Five percent.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he muttered "What's even the point"?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed, frustrated and full of dread about the results and the world.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with him, listened without arguing, and offered to go with him to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt hearing her brother talk like this?
qa.a: She may have felt worried but calm, wanting him to feel less alone.

grounding: During a power cut before results, a teenager voices a sense of dread and his sister supports him.

passage: In Porto, Ines, fifteen, had turned her bedroom into a turtle headquarters. Maps of the coast were taped to the wall, with red pins where people had found turtles tangled in fishing nets. Every Saturday she cycled to the beach with her friend Astrid to pick up plastic, even in the rain. She wrote to three local councillors. Two didn't answer. She kept writing. When Astrid said, "You talk about turtles more than anything," Ines laughed, but her eyes were bright. "Because nobody else is." At the beach clean-up that week, forty people came, many of them from her school. Ines stood on a rock, handing out bags, grinning so hard her face hurt.

qa.q: How many people came to the beach clean-up?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling when she stood on the rock handing out bags?
qa.a: She felt joyful and proud, full of energy for the cause she loves.

qa.q: How could Ines keep her passion going without burning out?
qa.a: She could share tasks with others at the clean-ups and take breaks, so the cause isn't all on her.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Ines's passion?
qa.a: Astrid finds it intense but seems to admire it and keeps joining her.

grounding: A Portuguese teenager's passion for saving turtles drives her campaigns and clean-ups.

passage: The robotics lab at the Pune school closed at six, but Vidya was there until the guard came to switch off the lights. Her team's robot kept turning left when it should go straight. Mr Mridul, the teacher in charge, found her crouched over the motor again. "You've been here every evening this week." "It's so close, Sir." Her hands were greasy, and there was a pencil behind her ear. "When it works, it'll be the best feeling." He sat down. "Show me what you've tried." She explained six changes, one after another, eyes lit up. He pointed at one wire. She tightened it. The robot rolled straight across the floor. Vidya jumped up so fast she knocked over a chair.

qa.q: What time did the robotics lab close?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the robot finally rolled straight?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and elated, jumping up so fast she knocked over a chair.

qa.q: What did Mr Mridul do that helped?
qa.a: He asked her to explain what she'd tried before pointing to the loose wire.

qa.q: How might Mr Mridul see Vidya staying late every evening?
qa.a: He seems impressed by her dedication, and perhaps a little concerned she's working too long.

grounding: A teenager's passion for robotics keeps her working late until her robot finally works.

passage:
Saturday. Sachin's diary.
The team list went up. I wasn't on it. Dolma asked if I was okay and I said, "Whatever, cricket's boring anyway." I even laughed. Then I went home and lay on my bed for two hours. The truth is I practised every evening for a month. If I say I don't care, then it doesn't look like I lost. That's the idea, anyway. But it doesn't make the heavy feeling go away. Dolma messaged later: "You're allowed to be upset, you know." I didn't reply. I'll maybe reply tomorrow. Or talk to Coach about what I can work on.

qa.q: How long did Sachin practise before the list went up?
qa.a: Every evening for a month.

qa.q: Why did Sachin tell Dolma "Whatever, cricket's boring anyway"?
qa.a: To hide feeling hurt and disappointed, so it wouldn't look like losing.

qa.q: What could Sachin do next instead of pretending not to care?
qa.a: Reply to Dolma honestly and ask Coach what to work on for next time.

qa.q: How might Dolma see Sachin's "whatever"?
qa.a: Dolma seems to see through it, gently telling Sachin it's okay to be upset.

grounding: A teenager's diary reveals pretending not to care about not being selected, to hide hurt.

passage: In Karad, Rafiq's father announced they were closing the cycle-repair shop and moving to Pune. Rafiq, fifteen, shrugged. "Fine. I don't care." At school, his teacher Minakshi Ma'am mentioned she'd heard. "It's nothing," he said, eyes on his desk. "It's just a shop." But at lunch he went and sat behind the shop, where he'd learned to fix punctures at eight. He ran his hand over the old air pump. Minakshi Ma'am, passing on her scooter, stopped. "You spent your childhood here, na?" Rafiq's throat went tight. "I don't want to cry about a shop." "It's not just a shop," she said. He nodded, finally, and let himself sit there a while.

qa.q: Where was the family moving?
qa.a: To Pune.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he said "It's nothing"?
qa.a: He felt sad and hurt about losing the shop but hid it behind detachment.

qa.q: What did Minakshi Ma'am do that helped Rafiq drop the act?
qa.a: She named what the shop meant to him instead of accepting his "I don't care."

qa.q: How might Rafiq's father feel if he knew how much the shop meant to Rafiq?
qa.a: He might feel touched and sad, and want to talk with his son about the move.

grounding: A small-town teenager feigns indifference about his family's shop closing to cover his sadness.
